items.title: University Hackathon by Miva Open University: Climate Risk and Health Prediction Challenge
items.text:
Host: Zindi
Location: Online
Starts: 20 October 2026, 04:00 UTC
Deadline: 6 November 2026, 23:59 UTC
Prize: 500 Points
Difficulty: Good for beginners
Skills: Prediction, Classification, Geospatial Data
Access: Zindi marks this competition as restricted.

Can you detect climate-linked patterns in mortality data?

Description

Health outcomes are shaped by more than biology alone. Age, living conditions, geography, and environmental factors can all influence vulnerability to illness and mortality. In many low-resource settings, changes in climate conditions such as rainfall and temperature can further increase health risks, particularly for vulnerable populations.

This challenge asks participants to explore the relationship between climate and health outcomes by building a supervised machine learning model that predicts whether a recorded death falls into a climate-sensitive category. Using health, demographic, geographic, and climate-related data, participants will identify patterns that can help improve our understanding of how environmental conditions may contribute to mortality.

The challenge provides an opportunity to apply classification, prediction, and geospatial machine learning to a real-world public health problem, with the broader goal of supporting data-driven approaches to understanding climate-related health risks.

Data Description

The dataset includes demographic information such as age and gender, along with location data in the form of district identifiers and/or geographic coordinates for each recorded death. The location information will enables participants to link mortality records to publicly available datasets.

Participants are encouraged to use publicly available climate datasets to enrich the training data. Permitted sources include temperature reanalysis products such as ERA5, rainfall datasets such as CHIRPS, and satellite-derived environmental indicators such as NDVI or land surface temperature.

All external datasets used must be publicly accessible. Participants are encouraged to share links to any external data sources on the competition forum to support transparency and reproducibility.

Some climate features have been downloaded and added to get you started. However you are welcome to download yours. A dictionary of these features is given in downloaded_climate_features_data_dictionary.csv

Evaluation

Your model must output:

- a binary target indicating whether the death is climate-sensitive or not
- a probability indicating the likelihood that the death is climate-sensitive

Setting a probability threshold is strictly forbidden. Your binary target should be based on the default threshold of 0.5.

The submission file should follow this format:

ID TargetF1 TargetRAUC

ID_XYZ4AL 0 0.45

ID_XTLAUX 0 0.32

where the values in the TargetF1 column correspond to the binary predictions and the values in the TargetRAUC column are the predicted probabilities. This format is required for multi-metric evaluation.

The challenge uses multi-metric evaluation. There are two error metrics: F1-Score and ROC-AUC. The final leaderboard score is the weighted average of the two metrics:

- F1-Score (60%): provides a suitable representation of a model's effectiveness by considering both precision and recall, which are crucial for imbalance datasets.
- ROC-AUC (40%): measures how well the model ranks climate-sensitive cases above non-climate-sensitive one across all possible thresholds. This provides a stable assessment of overall ranking for such an imbalanced dataset.

Rules

- Languages and tools: You may only use open-source languages and tools in building models for this challenge.
- Who can compete: Open to all
- Submission Limits: 10 submissions per day, 300 submissions overall.
- Team size: Max team size of 4

You may use only the datasets provided for this challenge as well as publicly available climate datasets.

You may use pretrained models as long as they are openly available to everyone.

Automated machine learning tools such as automl are not permitted.

items.title: Underwater Vessel Noise Challenge by the French Embassy in South Africa
items.text:
Host: Zindi
Location: Online
Starts: 16 October 2026, 12:00 UTC
Deadline: 13 December 2026, 12:00 UTC
Prize: $5 000 USD
Difficulty: Intermediate
Skills: Prediction, Classification, Feature Engineering, Time-series, Data analysis, Data visualisation

Can you help marine scientists detect and understand underwater vessel noise with machine learning?

Description

Ships and small boats produce underwater sound through their engines and propellers. This noise can affect marine animals that rely on hearing to navigate, feed and communicate. The challenge aims to help researchers monitor vessel-related noise along the South African coast and distinguish it from wind, waves and marine life.

The South African data come from hydrophones, or underwater microphones. You receive one-minute summaries of sound energy in different frequency bands, showing how energy varies from lower- to higher-pitched sounds; the original audio is not provided. AIS vessel-tracking data show the reported positions of nearby vessels, but do not confirm which vessel produced a sound. The South African measurements have no verified vessel-noise labels.

In this challenge, you will train on real data supplied by SAEON, SANBI, and the SA Underwater Radiated Noise Consortium (SA URN). Use these unlabelled South African measurements to develop and adapt models that recognise vessel-related acoustic patterns. Synthetic training data are not provided.

You may use public external acoustic datasets under their applicable licences. Share source links, versions and access instructions with the community through the challenge discussion board so other participants can obtain the same data. Redistribute files only where their licences permit it. You may adapt your methods using the South African data provided.

Since the real South African measurements do not have verified vessel-noise labels, the scored test uses controlled additions. Each test window combines real background measurements with an added vessel-sound component whose energy is known. This gives all models the same measurable target for comparison. Performance on this test must be supported by evidence on real data before claiming reliable vessel-noise monitoring.

For each test window, predict two values between 0 and 1: the fraction of total measured energy contributed by the added vessel component, and an evidence score indicating how strongly your model detects that component. For example, a predicted fraction of 0.20 means that the added component accounts for 20% of the window's measured energy. This target describes the controlled addition, not all vessel noise naturally present in the background.

Research write-ups should demonstrate how the model works on real South African measurements and produces a useful pressure map: a view of how vessel-related acoustic activity varies across monitoring sites and over time. Compare the map with observed acoustic patterns, explain uncertainty and show that the model responds to relevant signals rather than general noise. Without independent calibration, describe the map as relative acoustic activity. Supported interpretations of vessel number or size are an additional strength.

There are additional prizes for methodology or research write-ups.

SPONSORED BY:

French Embassy in South Africa, Lesotho and Malawi through Le Shift Lab:

The Embassy of France in South Africa, Lesotho and Malawi is the main sponsor of this challenge via its Le Shift Lab programme, a 2-year initiative to support green & digital transformation in Southern Africa and connect climate tech ecosystems with France. One of its components is specifically dedicated to cooperation on sustainable AI.

South African Environmental Observation Network (SAEON) The National Research Foundation’s South African Environmental Observation Network (NRF-SAEON) is a national research infrastructure dedicated to long-term environmental observation, research and data management. Through its network of observation sites, research platforms and data systems, SAEON collects, preserves and makes environmental data accessible to support scientific discovery, evidence-based decision-making and sustainable development.

SUPPORTED BY:

AI for Good - International Telecommunication Union (ITU)

AI for Good is organized by ITU in partnership with 40 UN Sister Agencies. The goal of AI for Good is to identify practical applications of AI to advance the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals and scale those solutions for global impact. It’s the leading action-oriented, global & inclusive United Nations platform on AI.

The South African National Biodiversity Institute (SANBI)

SANBI leads and coordinates research, and monitors and reports on the state of biodiversity in South Africa. The institute provides knowledge and information, gives planning and policy advice and pilots best-practice management models in partnership with stakeholders. SANBI engages in ecosystem restoration and rehabilitation, leads the human capital development strategy of the sector and manages the National Botanical and Zoological Gardens as ‘windows’ to South Africa’s biodiversity for enjoyment and education.

Coalition for Sustainable AI

The Coalition for Sustainable AI is an initiative coordinated by France, the UN Environment Programme and the International Telecommunication Union, with the support of several international organizations. Launched at the Paris AI Action Summit in 2025, it aims at building a global community of stakeholders willing to contribute to initiatives for aligning AI development with global sustainability goals and fostering responsible AI that supports the environmental policies.

This challenge will be integrated into the resources of the AI and Ocean vertical of the Coalition so as to further expand its potential for re-use and impact.

BioConsult SH

BioConsult SH GmbH & Co. KG is an independent ecological research and consulting company, based in Husum. Dr Georg Nehls founded the company in 1998. Since 2022, Dr Georg Nehls and Dr Thilo Liesenjohann are managing directors and partners.

Our work focuses on environmental planning and expert advice as well as ecological research and data collection.

What started as a three-person office in 1998 has now grown into an interdisciplinary and international team with over 160 employees. In addition to the two office locations in Husum, there is a further office in Hamburg Altona since 2024.

Evaluation

The leaderboard score is (1 − RMSE), where RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error) is calculated on share_added_vessel. Higher scores are better; a perfect prediction scores 1. Each test window contributes equally to RMSE.

share_added_vessel estimates the fraction of the window's total acoustic energy contributed by the controlled addition of a vessel-passage reference. The reference target is the sum of added passage-reference energy divided by the sum of total mixture energy. Both sums use the same observed minute-band cells across the 25 test bands, in linear energy units.

For example, 2 units of added passage-reference energy in a mixture containing 10 units gives a target of 0.20. This represents an energy fraction, not a probability. A target of zero means that no passage reference was added; the original background may still contain naturally occurring vessel sounds.

For every ID in sample_submission.csv, submit one row containing:

- share_added_vessel: your estimated added energy fraction.
- score_added_vessel: a continuous evidence score indicating whether a controlled vessel-passage addition is present.

Both predictions must be finite numbers between 0 and 1. Submit one value per output for the entire window, rather than separate predictions for individual minutes or frequency bands.

Only share_added_vessel determines the leaderboard score. score_added_vessel is collected for diagnostic analysis using ROC AUC and does not affect ranking. It should not be interpreted as a calibrated probability of natural vessel presence.

Your submission file should follow this format. The IDs and values below are illustrative only; use the actual IDs and column order from sample_submission.csv.

ID,share_added_vessel,score_added_vessel

EXAMPLE_A,0.20,0.50

EXAMPLE_B,0.00,0.30

The public leaderboard uses approximately 30% of the test examples. Final rankings are determined by (1 - RMSE) on the remaining 70%, used for private evaluation. Individual examples' public/private membership is not disclosed during the competition.

Pressure maps and evidence of performance on real South African data belong in the research write-up and do not contribute to the automated leaderboard score. Synthetic test performance alone does not establish accuracy on natural vessel activity.

Research write-ups

Research write-ups are expected to demonstrate high-quality model performance on real South African acoustic data and construct well-supported pressure maps. Claims must be backed by reproducible acoustic evidence, controls and uncertainty; synthetic rank or AIS proximity alone is insufficient.

- Evaluation: hold out released South African stations or periods from training and adaptation. Declare window identifiers, sample sizes and tuning.
- Acoustic evidence: align observed frequency-band signals and predictions. Include weak activity, interference, missing data and failures, with a summary of the full evaluated sample alongside selected examples.
- Controls: compare with received energy or another simple acoustic baseline. Use relevant spectral/time controls or ablations; if AIS informs the model, also show results without AIS.
- Pressure maps: provide maps of acoustic pressure or a clearly defined relative proxy, with coverage, time alignment, units, uncertainty and correspondence with observed signals. Validate any spatial interpolation. Distinguish total sound from inferred vessel contributions; physical-pressure or probability claims require calibration.
- Interpretability is a major plus: explain which acoustic features drive predictions. Independently validated estimates of simultaneous vessel number and size or size class add value. Report errors, uncertainty and AIS coverage limits. These are not scored synthetic targets.
- Accompanying code: each research write-up must include runnable code or notebooks that reproduce its analysis, figures and pressure maps. Provide dependency versions and clear execution instructions.
- Reproducibility: supply runnable analysis and outputs; uncertainty should account for repeated observations. Explain failures and what additional evidence would establish vessel identity or ship-only energy.

Review considers evidence quality, usefulness, uncertainty, reproducibility and efficiency. Unlabelled observations are not confirmed negatives. Demonstrated limitations are valuable; unsupported transfer or vessel-count/size claims do not qualify. Research write-ups will be submitted at the end of the challenge.

Prizes

🥇1st place: $1,500 USD + invitation to ChangeNOW Summit 2027 for one person to present your winning solution, worth $2,500 USD

🥈 2nd place: $1,000 USD

🥉 3rd place: $500 USD

📝 Best writeup: 2x $1,000

Data Description

For this challenge, you will work with real acoustic measurements from ten monitoring sites along South Africa’s coast. These data provide an opportunity to explore the local underwater soundscape and develop or adapt your models to South African recording conditions.

South African training data:

1,715,779 real, unlabelled acoustic records from ten sites, generally at one-minute resolution. These are frequency-band summaries, not audio recordings. There is no supplied vessel-label column or labelled Train.csv.

South_African_Real_Acoustics.zip contains one Parquet file per site in the acoustics/ directory, together with station metadata, recorder metadata and a data dictionary. Each acoustic table includes site/recorder identifiers, export timestamps (t), observed duration in seconds (dur), TOL_<frequency> band levels and basic quality flags. Recorder band coverage varies; quality flags are screening aids, not a guarantee of usable measurements.

Supporting files:

- stations.csv gives working coordinates and uncertainty notes
- recorders.csv gives recorder coverage; DATA_DICTIONARY.md explains the fields and known limitations.

Some additional notes:

- If you obtain AIS data separately, check its timestamp convention against the acoustic export clock before joining the datasets.
- Coordinates are approximate. If you use external AIS, its coverage may be incomplete and a single observation may be linked to more than one site.
- The absence of AIS data does not prove a vessel was absent, and proximity to a hydrophone does not prove it was audible.

Synthetic test data:

The test uses real South African background measurements with controlled additions derived from recorded vessel passages. Knowing the added energy lets us define a target even though the original measurements are unlabelled. Some windows have no added passage reference, and other acoustic activity can also be present. A zero target means no controlled addition; it does not mean the original background is vessel-free.

A passage reference may include ambient sound from its original recording. Its known added energy is therefore not isolated vessel-only energy. The test includes references from smaller craft and larger ships; vessel identity, count, type and size are not scored targets.

You receive 1,500 test examples in Test.csv. Each example represents a 15-minute observation window with measurements in 25 frequency bands. One CSV row contains its ID and all 375 acoustic values (15 minute positions × 25 bands). These are summaries of acoustic measurements, not raw audio samples.

The 25 bands are logarithmically spaced third-octave bands on a base-10 (deci-decade) grid. Their centre frequencies run from approximately 31.6 Hz to 7.94 kHz. These are band centres, not the outer edges of the frequency range.

Sound levels are expressed in decibels (dB), using the convention of the original exports. Absolute pressure calibration has not been independently verified. Decibels are logarithmic: adding two dB values does not give the combined sound energy. Missing observations are blank cells in Test.csv and will normally load as NaN. A finite value is observed; a blank cell is missing and must not be treated as silence. No separate validity-mask file is required.

All test examples are supplied together in a random order, identified only by ID. You are not told which examples belong to public or private evaluation. Test windows do not include station locations, observation timestamps or AIS tracks, and the original backgrounds before the additions are not provided. The background periods used for the test are excluded from the training release.

Test files:

- Test.csv contains all 1,500 test windows. Its columns are ID followed by 375 acoustic features, ordered by minute position and then frequency. For example, m01_TOL_31.6 is the band centred at 31.6 Hz at minute position 1. Band centres and minute positions are encoded in the column names; minute positions are relative to the window, not observation timestamps.
- SampleSubmission.csv contains all 1,500 test IDs and the required columns: ID, share_added_vessel and score_added_vessel. Prediction values are placeholders, not answers.
- maritime_starter_notebook.ipynb shows how to load the CSV files, recover the 15-minute × 25-band layout and create a valid constant-baseline submission. It also includes source attribution and licence notices.

Participants may learn from released real South African measurements and permitted public corpora, using labelled external examples where available, self-supervised methods, carefully qualified AIS supervision, or their own augmentations. No particular method is required.

You may use public acoustic data from Ocean Networks Canada (ONC) and Croatia's HearMyShip, subject to the competition's external-data rules. These datasets are not included in the download package; obtain them directly from their providers.

If you use external audio recordings, convert them to the one-minute frequency-band representation expected by the test inputs. Explain how you handle measurement units, time alignment and missing observations, so others can reproduce your work.

Location: Online
Starts: 26 October 2026, 12:00 UTC

Difficulty: Beginners
Skills: Classification, Visualisation, Data analysis, Data storytelling

Can you use AI to map Mumbai’s air quality and predict pollution?

Description

YT:H_RD-X4-6WU

Register for the Challenge

Ready to take on the Google Mumbai Data Challenge?

Register below to join:

Complete the Google Mumbai Data Challenge Registration Form

Air pollution is one of India's most pressing environmental and public health challenges. Across the country, millions of people are exposed to harmful levels of airborne pollutants, with air quality changing dramatically between cities, seasons, and even hours of the day.

From traffic congestion and industrial emissions to changing weather patterns and seasonal agricultural burning, many factors influence the air we breathe. These complex interactions make air pollution difficult to predict, but they also create an opportunity for machine learning to make a meaningful difference. What if we could predict dangerous pollution levels before they occur?

Accurate air quality forecasts could help communities take precautions, enable authorities to respond proactively, and support smarter environmental planning. In this challenge, your task is to develop a machine learning model that forecasts hourly PM2.5 concentrations across monitoring stations in Mumbai, using historical air quality observations.

You will work with real-world environmental monitoring data sourced from India's Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), which operates a nationwide air quality monitoring network. The data captures changes in atmospheric pollutant concentrations over time, providing an opportunity to explore how pollution patterns evolve across different locations and environmental conditions. Your goal is to uncover these patterns and build a model that can accurately predict future pollution concentrations using information available up to the time of prediction.

Relevance of the Solution

Solutions developed through this challenge could demonstrate how data science and AI can contribute to environmental monitoring and urban decision-making.

By identifying spatial patterns and forecasting changes in air quality, participants can explore approaches that may support environmental research, public awareness and longer-term planning for healthier, more sustainable cities.

The challenge also provides participants with an opportunity to build practical machine-learning skills while working on a real-world environmental problem.

The challenge is open to participants across India. However, to qualify as a finalist and be considered for an invitation to the closing event, participants must be residents of Maharashtra. Proof of Maharashtra residency will be requested during finalist verification.

Google

Google is a global technology company whose mission is to make information universally accessible and useful. Through its work in AI and technology, Google supports innovation and the development of solutions to real-world challenges.

Beyond

Beyond is Google's programme partner for this challenge, working with Zindi to coordinate the programme and support the delivery of the Mumbai Data Challenge.

Climateverse

Climateverse is an AI-powered, open-source platform that makes climate data easier to find, trust and use. It is led by CrisisReady at Harvard with support from the Mittal South Asia Institute and the Harvard Data Science Initiative.

The platform brings together curated datasets across climate, agriculture, socioeconomics, health and more. Each dataset is reviewed by local experts and comes with clear information about its coverage, reliability and access.

Users can spend less time searching scattered portals and more time answering the questions that matter to them. By combining AI with local knowledge, Climateverse helps communities, researchers and policymakers find the evidence they need to understand climate risks and plan adaptation.

Evaluation

Submissions are evaluated using Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), which measures how closely predicted hourly PM2.5 concentrations match actual measurements. Larger errors receive a greater penalty. Lower scores are better.

The final submission deadline is 10 November 2026 at 23:59:59 IST. The latest valid submission will be evaluated on the private period, 11–12 November. Final rankings will use private RMSE, subject to code review and compliance with the competition rules.

Prize

- 1st place: $2,500 USD
- 2nd place: $1,500 USD
- 3rd place: $1,000 USD

Other Categories:

- Best undergraduate student: $500
- Best additional submission: $500

There are 5 000 Zindi points available. You can read more about Zindi points here.

Finalist eligibility: While participation is open across India, only Maharashtra residents are eligible to qualify among the finalists invited to the closing event. Finalist residency will be verified before invitations are issued.

Data Description

The challenge uses historical observations from the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), collected through India’s Continuous Ambient Air Quality Monitoring Stations (CAAQMS).

Participants will predict hourly PM2.5 concentrations (µg/m³) at four monitoring stations in Mumbai. Predictions will be evaluated against new observations as they become available.

Training data updates

Train.csv will be updated on 31 October, 5 November and 9 November, with a final update scheduled for 10 November at 09:00 IST. Participants may use newly released observations to retrain their models and update predictions.

Test and submissions

Test.csv and SampleSubmission.csv contain the same 2,592 IDs throughout the competition. IDs, station-hours, row count and row order remain fixed.

Every submission must contain the columns ID and Target, with a non-negative PM2.5 prediction for every ID, in the original row order.

Public leaderboard updates

At launch on 26 October, the public score will use observations for 22–23 October, excluded from the launch Train.csv. This window remains active until the 31 October update. Subsequent updates will use:

- 31 October update: observations for 27–28 October.
- 5 November update: observations for 1–2 November.
- 9 November update: observations for 5–6 November.

Only the current two-day window contributes to the public score. Each update replaces the previous scoring window; earlier periods no longer contribute. The test files remain unchanged, and participants may continue submitting updated predictions until the final submission deadline.

All dates are in 2026, using IST (UTC+05:30). Data and leaderboard updates depend on measurement availability.

Starter Notebook

Get started with the data, train a simple Random Forest model, and create your first submission.

Explore Additional Datasets

Looking to improve your air quality forecasts? Explore ClimateVerse’s Google Air Quality Forecasting Challenge page to discover additional climate and environmental datasets that may help inform your modelling approach.
